analysis.one_liner: Strips greenhouse gases out of the Clean Air Act so they can't be regulated.
analysis.headline: A single-sponsored bill to exempt greenhouse gases from Clean Air Act regulation never advanced past a House subcommittee and got no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Clean Air Act to say carbon dioxide, methane, and other greenhouse gases are not "air pollutants," and would declare that the Act cannot be used to regulate climate change. In 2007 the Supreme Court had ruled the Act covers greenhouse gases, so this would remove the EPA's main legal tool for limiting emissions from power plants and other large polluters. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy and Power subcommittee, where it sat until the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Power plants, oil and gas producers, and other large emitters of greenhouse gases, because they would face no federal limits on carbon pollution under the Clean Air Act.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fossil fuel producers and large emitters

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Clean Air Act's definition of "air pollutant" to exclude carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, hydrofluorocarbons, perfluorocarbons, and sulfur hexafluoride, the main greenhouse gases [S2][S3].
Adds a blanket statement that nothing in the Clean Air Act authorizes or requires regulation of climate change or global warming, blocking any EPA climate rules under the Act [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public: greenhouse gas emissions from power plants and industry would go unregulated at the federal level under the Clean Air Act, leaving the costs of climate change to fall on everyone.

drawbacks.text: Removing the EPA's Clean Air Act authority over greenhouse gases would leave no federal backstop for carbon emissions from power plants and large industrial sources [S2][S3].
The bill is a one-line carve-out rather than a replacement policy; it eliminates climate regulation under the Act without putting any alternative limits or programs in its place [S3].

Supporters would argue it prevents regulatory costs on energy producers and electricity prices; the bill contains no provisions addressing those costs or any transition for affected industries or workers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The only clear beneficiaries are large emitters, who avoid federal carbon limits. The public bears the cost of unregulated emissions, and the bill offers no substitute policy, so what it takes away is not balanced by anything it provides.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then its Energy and Power subcommittee, and no vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Henry Cuellar, a Texas Democrat, introduced the bill on March 31, 2011 [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction [S5].
On April 7, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power, and no further action followed for the rest of the 112th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public is better off that the bill never advanced, since passing it would have stripped the EPA's Clean Air Act authority over greenhouse gases. Fossil fuel producers and large emitters lost the chance at that exemption.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public; emitters lost their shot at an exemption

for.name: Henry Cuellar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt greenhouse gases from the Clean Air Act.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took the referral and forwarded it to the Energy and Power subcommittee, where it received no markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so no partisan breakdown exists; notably, a Democrat sponsored the bill with no support from either party.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel producers and coal-fired power plants
industries.note: The bill would exempt their carbon emissions from all Clean Air Act limits, removing the EPA's main tool for regulating them. That gain comes directly at the public's expense in the form of unregulated emissions.
Like power plants, these facilities would face no federal greenhouse gas limits under the Act, avoiding compliance costs that would otherwise fall on them.
